newsitem.title: USA: Enron, PGE merger concerns raised. [CORRECTED 20:50 GMT 30/10]
newsitem.headline: Enron, PGE merger concerns raised. [CORRECTED 20:50 GMT 30/10]

text.p: Enron Corp's planned purchase of Portland General Electric Co (PGE) has raised concerns among some industry participants about market dominance and fair competition.
But Enron officials insist the merger should be reviewed on its own merits, not in terms of ongoing restructuring of the electricity industry.
Historically operated as regulated monopolies, the U.S. natural gas and, more recently, electricity industries, are being deregulated with the aim of reducing rates for consumers.
The Enron-Portland deal, announced in July, was heralded as the start of a trend driven by opportunities to boost efficiency amid "convergence" of energy markets.
Natural gas is a key fuel for electricity generation as well as a primary energy source.

"There is a complementary relationship between our organizations," said Geoff Roberts, managing director of Enron Capital & Trade Resources. "The concerns that have been raised are mostly about uncertainties in the deregulation process."

The companies' shareholders are scheduled to vote November 12 on the deal which, if approved, would give Portland's shareholders one share of Enron common for each share of Portland General share. Enron would also assume $1.1 billion of Portland's debt.
The deal also must be approved by the Oregon Public Utilities Commission and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in Washington DC.
Over the past couple of weeks comments have been filed with both agencies by a range of interested parties.

San Francisco-based Pacific Gas & Electric Co, for instance, says Portland General should be barred from selling federal preference power outside of the Northwest as a condition of its proposed merger with Enron.

In a filing to FERC, Pacific Gas said electricity from the Bonneville Power Administration is intended for use by public utilities in the Northwest and should not be made available to Enron or other marketing affiliates outside the region.

Steve Kean, with Enron Capital & Trade, regulatory affairs, emphasized that the merger is structured so that Portland General will continue to be a regulated utility, subject to existing public service commitments at both state and federal levels.

"Deregulation of the retail market is already the subject of statewide and regional reviews as well as a number of federal legislative proposals," he noted. "This transaction is not the place to deal with that issue."

Pacific Gas (corrects company name from Portland General), which said it neither supports nor opposes the merger, cited other conditions it believes need to be implemented such as oversight of access to Pacific Gas transmission.
The Oregon Public Utilities Commission began its review of the merger in September. So far, there have been more than 30 intervenors in the case, a commission spokesman said last week.

Other utilities expressing concern over the merger include PacifiCorp, Washington Water Power Co, Enova Corp's San Diego Gas and Electric Co, Edison International's Southern California Edison Co, and Northwest Natural Gas Co.
Their concerns include worries that terms of the deal might hinder competition or that Enron might be able to shift costs from unregulated activities to a regulated Portland General.
